title: Query Optimization & Execution
relevance: Interviewers use this to separate candidates who guess at SQL performance from those who can reason about plans, indexes, and why a query suddenly got slow.

phases.goal: Establish that SQL states what data is wanted and the engine decides how via Parser, Optimizer, and Executor.

must_hit.point: A SQL query describes what data you want, not how to retrieve it; the database engine figures out the how.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts declarative SQL with the engine choosing a retrieval strategy.

must_hit.point: Every query goes through Parser (syntax/semantics/permissions), Optimizer (generate plans and pick the estimated fastest), then Executor (run the plan against storage).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three phases in order and gives each a one-line job.

must_hit.point: The optimizer produces multiple possible execution plans and chooses the one it estimates will be fastest.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions multiple candidate plans and cost/estimate-based selection, not a single fixed path.

probes: Walk through what happens from the moment you submit a SQL query until rows come back.

hints.1: Think about checking the query is valid before any data is read.
hints.2: There are three main phases: one validates, one plans, one runs.
hints.3: Parser → Optimizer (multiple plans, pick fastest estimate) → Executor against the storage engine.

phases.goal: Establish how to read plans: scan/join operators, EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and cost-based optimization driven by statistics.

must_hit.point: An execution plan is a tree of operators; data flows from leaf nodes upward, each operator a physical algorithm to retrieve or combine data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes bottom-up operator tree, not just a flat list of steps.

must_hit.point: Seq Scan reads every table page; Index Scan walks a B-Tree then visits the heap; Index Only Scan serves from the index alone when it covers the SELECT columns.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes full-table read, index-then-heap, and cover-from-index-only.

must_hit.point: Nested Loop probes the inner set per outer row; Hash Join builds a hash on the smaller set and probes from the larger; Merge Join steps through two join-column-sorted sets together.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all three joins with when each fits (small+indexed outer, large unsorted, already ordered).

must_hit.point: EXPLAIN shows the estimated plan without running the query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes it and reports real timing and row counts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Clearly separates estimate-only EXPLAIN from execute-and-measure EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

must_hit.point: A Cost-Based Optimizer estimates CPU, memory, and I/O cost using statistics such as row counts, distinct values, and distribution histograms; PostgreSQL ANALYZE (often via autovacuum) refreshes them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties plan choice to stats metadata and mentions ANALYZE/autovacuum for updates.

must_hit.point: For many index matches, Bitmap Index Scan builds a bitmap of heap blocks, then Bitmap Heap Scan reads those blocks sequentially—useful for ranges or combining indexes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains bitmap-then-heap to avoid random I/O per matching row.

probes: What do Seq Scan, Index Scan, and Index Only Scan each do, and how do Nested Loop, Hash Join, and Merge Join differ?

hints.1: Start with how rows are read from a table or index, then how two sets are combined.
hints.2: Scans: every page vs B-Tree+heap vs index-only; joins: per-outer probe vs hash build/probe vs sorted merge.
hints.3: Also mention EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE and that the CBO picks plans using table statistics updated by ANALYZE.

phases.goal: Establish when the optimizer prefers one scan or join strategy over another based on selectivity, size, and ordering.

must_hit.point: If most rows match (e.g. 99% status active), Seq Scan can beat Index Scan because the index plus heap is more work than reading the table; if few match (e.g. 1% active), Index Scan is cheaper.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses selectivity: dense matches → seq scan; sparse → index, with the 99%/1% active example.

must_hit.point: Nested Loop fits a very small outer set with an indexed inner join column; Hash Join is the go-to for large unsorted sets; Merge Join shines when both sides are already ordered on the join column.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps each join to size/ordering conditions without claiming one is always best.

must_hit.point: Rule-based optimizers always prefer an index when one exists; cost-based optimizers use live statistics and may reject the index when a seq scan is cheaper.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts historical RBO rules with CBO cost estimates from stats.

probes: When would the optimizer choose a sequential scan even though an index exists on the filter column?

hints.1: Think about how many rows actually match the predicate.
hints.2: Compare reading the whole table once versus reading the index and then most of the heap.
hints.3: If ~99% of rows match (e.g. status active), Seq Scan wins; if ~1% match, Index Scan wins—CBO uses stats for that call.

phases.goal: Apply plan literacy to SARGable predicates, expression indexes, bulk-load stats, and common SQL anti-patterns.

must_hit.point: A query is SARGable if the engine can use a B-Tree via ordered operators (=, >, <); wrapping the indexed column in a function, arithmetic, or a leading wildcard forces evaluation per row and a Seq Scan.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines SARGable and gives at least one non-SARGable pattern (function/arithmetic/leading %).

must_hit.point: An expression index (e.g. on UPPER(name)) can make a matching functional predicate SARGable again.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says create an index on the expression so WHERE UPPER(name) = ... can use it.

must_hit.point: After a massive load (e.g. inserting 10 million rows) without updating stats, the CBO may still think the table has ~1,000 rows and pick Nested Loop instead of Hash Join, turning a ~1 second query into minutes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links stale stats after bulk insert to wrong join choice and sudden slowdown; mentions ANALYZE.

must_hit.point: Common anti-patterns: SELECT * blocks Index Only Scans; correlated subqueries run per outer row (N+1); DISTINCT papers over a bad join; ORDER BY + LIMIT without an index sorts all rows before returning a few.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names several anti-patterns with the right fix direction (project columns, JOIN rewrite, fix join/EXISTS, index the order key).

probes: A query is slow even after you added an index—what do you check next, and how do you confirm with EXPLAIN?

hints.1: Ask whether the index can actually be used for the WHERE clause as written.
hints.2: Look for functions/casts on the column, leading wildcards, stale stats after bulk loads, and anti-patterns like SELECT * or correlated subqueries.
hints.3: Use EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE: non-SARGable predicates → Seq Scan; fix with SARGable rewrite or expression index; run ANALYZE after bulk changes; rewrite correlated subqueries as joins.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefer Seq Scan when most of the table must be read (e.g. 99% match) because index+heap is extra work; prefer Index Scan when few rows match (e.g. 1%). CBO decides from statistics, not from index existence alone.

tradeoffs.topic: Nested Loop vs Hash Join vs Merge Join
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Nested Loop for small outer + indexed inner; Hash Join for large unsorted inputs (hash the smaller side); Merge Join when both sides are already sorted on the join key.
RBO applies fixed rules (e.g. always use an index if present); CBO estimates CPU/memory/I/O from statistics and may choose Seq Scan over an index when that is cheaper.

tradeoffs.topic: Filter in the database vs fetch-all and filter in the app
tradeoffs.strong_answer: App-side filtering abandons DB indexes, incurs large network transfer, and moves CPU to the app server; keep predicates SARGable in SQL so the optimizer can use indexes.

tradeoffs.topic: Bitmap Heap path vs per-row Index Scan visits
tradeoffs.strong_answer: When many rows match via the index, Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan batches heap blocks for sequential access and can combine multiple indexes, avoiding random I/O per row.

gotchas.trap: Assuming an existing index means the optimizer will use it.
gotchas.correction: CBO may pick Seq Scan when selectivity is high; also non-SARGable predicates (functions, arithmetic, leading wildcards, casts) disable B-Tree use.

gotchas.trap: Query that was ~1 second yesterday now takes minutes with no SQL change.
gotchas.correction: Often stale statistics after a bulk load (e.g. 10 million inserts while planner still thinks ~1,000 rows)—wrong plan like Nested Loop instead of Hash Join; run ANALYZE (autovacuum may lag).

gotchas.trap: Adding an index but the query stays slow.
gotchas.correction: Check SARGability: rewrite EXTRACT/LEFT/casts/arithmetic off the column, or add an expression index that matches the predicate.
Prevents Index Only Scans unless the index covers every column; project only needed columns.

gotchas.trap: Correlated subquery counting related rows per parent.
gotchas.correction: Runs the inner query per outer row (N+1); rewrite as a JOIN so Hash/Merge joins can be used.

gotchas.trap: Using DISTINCT to clean up duplicate join results.
gotchas.correction: Usually masks a wrong one-to-many join; fix the join or use EXISTS instead of DISTINCT as a band-aid.

gotchas.trap: ORDER BY … LIMIT without an index on the sort key.
gotchas.correction: Engine sorts the full set then takes the limit; index the ordered column (e.g. created_at DESC) so it can stop early.

gotchas.trap: Leading-wildcard LIKE '%son' hoping for an index.
gotchas.correction: Cannot be SARGable on a normal B-Tree—sort order does not help when the first character is unknown.
